reallife_guide_utilities_about: Power, water and internet bills for every place you rent or own, the utilities office, and the Utilities app.
reallife_guide_utilities: Every home and business you rent or own uses power and water, and some need the internet. Accounts, bills and plans are in the Utilities app on your phone. # Power and water - City Light and Power and Riverside Water are run from the utilities office ({util_office}), which lights up on the city map. - A rented place has the landlord's accounts: it is supplied from the first day and you just pay the bills. - A place you buy needs accounts of its own. It is supplied for {util_temporary_days} days at {util_surcharge} more; apply in person at the office's desk before then, or the supply is cut. While no building can hold the office (every one that could is yours), the Utilities app takes applications and reconnections by phone instead, at the same prices, until a building is free again. An account connects the next morning. A poor credit rating asks for a deposit of one or two months, given back after {util_deposit_back} bills paid on time; a good one asks for none. - What a place uses follows its floor, the kind of business, the people living there and the season: heating in winter, cooling in summer. Power is {util_kwh} a kWh and {util_standing_power} a day, water {util_m3} a cubic metre and {util_standing_water} a day, at today's prices. - Without power a business closes, and so does one that needs water without it (food and drink, salons, gyms). At home a cut weighs on your mood: with no water the shower and the sink are dry, so you cannot wash, and with no power there are no screens and no cooking. # Bills - The month is billed at its turn, due in {util_due} days. Auto debit in the Utilities app pays a bill on its due day; otherwise pay it in the app or at the desk. A bill a day overdue has {util_late_fee} added; {util_cut_after} days after its due day the supply is cut, and reconnecting costs {util_reconnect_fee} as well. - The Planner shows each bill's due day, the day an unpaid one is cut and the day a temporary supply ends; the Finance app lists what is owed, and a partner or a roommate pays a share of the bills with the rent. # The internet - The internet comes from rival providers, bought in the Utilities app: {net_providers}. Each has its own plans and speeds, prices that move month by month, and its own reliability. An engineer installs a plan {net_install_days} days after it is bought. - On a contract of {net_contract_months} months the price is held and the installation is free; month by month it costs {net_monthly} more, and the installation {net_install_fee}. Leaving a contract early costs {net_exit} of each month left. A business plan costs {net_business} more and is repaired in half the time. - An outage lasts {net_outage_least} to {net_outage_most} hours in the daytime; a day with an outage is not charged. - Graphic designers, web development agencies, the tech firms (software and game studios, IT consultancies, cybersecurity firms and AI labs) and your headquarters cannot open without a connection, nor during an outage. Those you already had when the internet first came into your save were given {net_grace_days} days to get connected, with the days left in the Utilities app; one started since needs a connection from its first day. - A home's connection serves Newsstand, online classes, days worked from home and video interviews. One that an outage keeps you from is excused. # Speed (option: 'Internet speed matters') - Speed matters for tech firms and online shops; for everything else a connection is just on or off. Each plan's speed falls in a tier, and each step up a provider's list lifts the work a tier. - A tech firm's building, design, web and testing work goes at a pace set by its office's plan, as a share of its usual pace: {net_speed_work}. A game studio leans on its line half as much again and an AI lab twice as much (from {net_speed_ai_least} on the slowest line to {net_speed_ai_most} on the fastest); an IT consultancy or a graphic designer half as much. - An online shop takes as many orders a day as its building's plan allows, as a share of what its site could take: {net_speed_shop}. With no connection, or during an outage, an online shop takes no orders; shops you already had when speed first counted in your save were given {net_grace_days} days. - The Utilities app's plan picker says what each plan means at the place. With the option off, only having a connection counts. # Your own broadband company - Late in the game and very costly. With a headquarters, the city's operator's licence costs {bb_licence}; then each district's fibre costs {bb_build_least} to {bb_build_most} and is dug in {bb_build_months} of the game's months. - Where your network is open it is one of the providers: your own places connect free, and the district's homes and businesses choose it month by month by its prices against the usual, how rarely it fails (the maintenance you pay for), its marketing, and a name the district trusts a little more each month for {bb_trust_months} months. The rivals keep their prices down where it takes their customers. - Its takings and costs are booked at your headquarters, so its statement, the tax and the bank count them; without a headquarters it cannot bill anybody. A buyer pays {bb_sale_multiple} years of the last year's profit.

reallife_changes_003_0: The staff rota planner counts the goods. Where a Delivery Contract or a Logistics Manager brings a product, a plan sells it only while some is there, so no plan counts sales the shelves cannot supply. The Rota page names the goods that run out, when, what that costs a week, and what would keep them on the shelves: a larger delivery, more storage shelves, an Urgent Order, a second wholesaler or a higher target for the Logistics Manager. Fixed: the search box of the Contacts app stood off to the left of the app, out of sight; it now has a line of its own above the list. Fixed: the minimap turned with the way you walked; it now turns with the camera, and its arrow shows which way you face. Fixed: a car towed near the hospital after a crash (or out of a police impound) could stay where it was to the eye, with its marker on the map, while you walked through it and could not get in; the whole car now goes to the space. Fixed: the game could freeze for two seconds as an ambulance crew got out with the stretcher at an accident; the way they wheel it is now worked out in a moment. Bus stops: Choose a stop now opens the city map, as a subway entrance does. Every stop the buses reach is marked on it, and the game's list of stations beside it lists them with the line, the time and the fare, with a search field. Point at a stop to see it; click it to pick it. Fixed: at a subway entrance the mod's own list of stations had taken the place of the game's subway map. A click on the entrance opens the game's map again, and the mod adds the time of the journey when you come up. A day pass gives the game's fare back. The nightly closure of one station for track work is gone. On the city map, the mod's buildings now light up when their row is ticked, the way the game's own buildings do for theirs: police stations, the courthouse, hotels, driving schools, the buildings with a help-wanted board, polling places and construction sites, each in its row's colour and with its icon. The courthouse's card names it, with its hours. One calendar: a month is now a twelfth of the year you chose for your game (5 days in a 60-day year, 30 in a 365-day one), and the seasons are the weather's everywhere. Car insurance runs a month; childcare and private school are named by that month and paid by the week, at the same cost by the day as before; hotels and property follow the weather's seasons. Wages follow prices once: the city's cost of living pays every wage at today's prices, and the going rate staff compare their pay with is at today's prices too, so rising prices no longer make staff ask for raises on top. The city's wage floor counts any raise you agreed and moves with prices, and every amount of the city government (levies, grants, the licence fee, the ticket and fare changes, donations and shop refits) is at today's prices. Your businesses' books: the wages, marketing and licences of the Company features now show in the game's own daily statement of each business (EconoView, the daily summary), and the game's bank sizes a loan by that profit. Insurance, accountants and hosting, for which the game's statement has no line, stay in the Finance app. Fixed: a parking ticket on a lent car (the driving school's, a hired van) is paid back whole, the city policy's change to it included. The city's business tax share applies only where the game charges income tax at all. The pound charges one fee whatever the car was taken for, and the roadside tow is the hospital tow's. A partner's and a roommate's share of the rent is of what the home costs at today's prices. An online shop's takings follow prices as a shop's takings do. Life events about a credit card or an accountant happen only to somebody who has one. Every price follows the city's prices: fines and fees, fares and taxis, bail, lawyers and court costs, garage and car costs, bikes, clothes, drinks, family costs, hotels and trips, the banks' smallest loans and limits, and the pay of jobs and gigs are all at today's prices, and nothing moves while prices are within 1% of where they began. The game's own fixed charges (tickets and rides, the hospital and the doctor, gyms, shops and fuel, fit-outs, training and hiring) are adjusted on one line each night, Shops and services, cost of living adjustment, as rent and wages are; what you buy at a wholesaler's is left out, as the city prices those goods already. A ride the day pass covers and a lent car's ticket are paid back exactly as the game took them. The Guide, prompts, life events and the licence quiz name today's figures. The city's cost of living lines are booked to each business and home they belong to, so each business's statement in EconoView, the game's taxes and its bank's loan limit count them; the insurance premium and the rota planner take a shop's takings at today's prices once. Power and water: every home and business you rent or own has power and water bills from City Light and Power and Riverside Water, by its floor, its kind of business, who lives there and the season, at today's prices. A rented place just pays; a place you buy is supplied for three days at half as much again and then cut, unless you apply in person at the utilities office, which lights up on the map. A poor credit rating asks for a deposit. Bills come each month, and the Utilities app pays them by auto debit or by hand; a late bill has a fee and is cut three days after it was due, and reconnecting costs a fee. Without power a business closes, as does one that needs water without it; at home a cut means no shower, sink, screens or cooking, and weighs on your mood. Partners and roommates pay a share of the bills with the rent, the Finance app lists bills owed, and the Planner shows when each falls due and when an unpaid one is cut. Internet: four rival providers sell it in the Utilities app, each with its own reach, plans, reliability and prices that move month by month; on a contract or month by month, installed two days later. Web design and software companies and your headquarters cannot open without a connection, nor during an outage, and a day with an outage is not charged. Your own broadband company, late in the game and very costly: with a headquarters and the city's operator's licence, dig its fibre district by district, win the city's homes and businesses from the four providers by price, reliability and marketing while they answer with lower prices, its takings and costs in your headquarters' books, and sell it when you like. A business's power, water and internet bills are deducted by the tax. Every table of figures in the mod's apps now sorts and totals them, and no figure colours its cell any more. Your hotels and car hire pay the game's tax on their yearly profit, and the estate agency's commissions are taxed with your businesses' sales.

reallife_guide_markets_about: A stock market of the city's companies in its own Stocks app: prices that answer to everything in the city, candle charts and the analysis tools, orders of every usual kind (large ones worked over the market's steps), a margin account, property trusts that pay every few days, bonds and bank deposits that can roll over, and a portfolio that shows what each holding is and what it pays.
reallife_guide_markets: # The market - The Stocks app is on your phone. {mkt_companies} of the city's companies are listed, in {mkt_sectors} sectors, with the game's own rivals beside them and each rival tycoon's holding company once its tycoon comes forward (see 'Rival tycoons'). They trade on market days, Monday to Friday, from {mkt_open} to {mkt_close}. Prices move every {mkt_step} game minutes, and the night between two sessions is a gap. - A price is what the market makes of a company's business: what it is expected to pay out, discounted at the city's bank rate and a premium for its risk. News moves it and stays; the market's mood fades over the years. - Everything in the city moves it: the economy's cycle and the bank rate, inflation and prices, the supply of goods, the council's policies and elections, the weather and street events, crime, fires and accidents, and the takings of your own businesses in the same trade. - Each quarter a company gives its results before the open, and the price answers at the open. The dividend is declared with them: whoever holds shares at the close of the record day, {mkt_record_days} market days later, is paid {mkt_pay_days} market days after that, and the price drops by the dividend the next morning. Each dividend paid to you or your bots is a line of the market news, with a notification of the amount, one for all that come at once. - {mkt_trusts} of the companies are property trusts, which own buildings and let them. A trust pays out at least {mkt_trust_payout} of its profit, in small sums every week or every third day: whoever holds its shares at the close of a period's last market day is paid on the next market day, and the price drops by the payment the next morning. {mkt_trust_property} of a trust's worth is its buildings, valued where the city's property market is heading; the rest is its rents, which follow prices, what households earn and the council's rent policy. - Companies split their shares when the price passes {mkt_split}, are bid for at a premium of {mkt_premium_least} to {mkt_premium_most} ({mkt_fail} of bids fall through), have crises and windfalls, and now and then fail. New companies come to the market. Shares that trade under {mkt_penny} for {mkt_penny_days} market days leave the market at their last price. # Trading - On a company's page the order ticket has Buy and Sell and four kinds. At the market is filled at once, at the offer to buy and at the bid to sell; a Limit only at its price or better; a Stop loss and a Take profit close what you hold once the price reaches theirs. An order lasts For the day or Until cancelled, {mkt_good_till} market days at most, and {mkt_orders_most} can be open at once. Before you place it, it shows the price, the commission and how far its size moves the price. The page 'Orders and trading bots' says how each kind works. - Every purchase and sale costs {mkt_commission} in commission, {mkt_commission_least} at least, besides the spread between the bid and the offer. A large order moves the price against itself, the more against a day's usual volume, and splitting it saves nothing. - One order can be for at most {mkt_order_share} of a day's usual volume. You can hold at most {mkt_holding} of a company's shares, as 'The most of a company you may hold' is set ({mkt_holding_own} unless you change it, up to all of it). A rival tycoon's holding company stops at {mkt_holding_float}, the part its tycoon does not own, and a player's listed company at {mkt_holding_own}. Lowered, a holding already past it is kept; only new buying is refused. With 'Worked orders and larger bond purchases' on, a larger order at the market is worked over the market's steps instead: the ticket says so, and Work it places it. - On a company's page you choose how much of each dividend it pays you goes back into the same company: none, a quarter, half, three quarters or all of what is left after the tax withheld. It buys shares at the next open, a purchase like any other, within one order's most and the most you may hold (the rest stays in your cash); the History tab marks it. - An order placed while the market is shut waits for the open. After a load no order is taken until the market is back at the furthest moment it has reached, so nothing seen before the load can be traded on. # The Stocks app - Market: the city index and every sector's, with their moves over a day, a week, a month and longer, the market's state, the bank rate and the news. Companies: every listed company, sorted by any column (price, the day's move, volume, worth, P/E, yield) and narrowed by sector and size. Then Watchlist (up to {mkt_watch_most} companies, added with Watch on a company's page), Orders, Portfolio, History, Bots, Bonds and Futures (see 'Futures and options'). - Pick a company for its page. Chart: candles of today, days, weeks, months or years with its volume (the wheel zooms, a drag moves through time, the pointer shows each candle), moving averages or Bollinger bands over it, and RSI, MACD, the stochastic, the average true range or on-balance volume under it. Figures: worth, turnover, profit and margin, earnings and P/E, book value, debt, the dividend and how much of the earnings it pays out, the next results and its finances, with its last results against what was expected. - Portfolio: everything you hold, each marked with what it is (a stock, a property trust, a Treasury bond, a city bond or a deposit at a bank), your bots' shares and your own company's stake marked as such, with what it cost and is worth, its gain, what it has paid and its next payment, and Today's change of it all since the last close. Filter it by sector or by kind. Its box has three pages: What you hold, the spread across kinds with your cash; What it pays over the next year before tax, with its yield and the next payments; and Your account. - Bonds: the bonds and bank deposits on offer, the Treasury ladder, and yours, with their price and next payment. A property trust's page says what it pays and when. # In the paper and the Planner - The City Ledger reports each close: its markets page has the market's stories, the index, every sector and the day's movers, and its share prices every company. Its front page carries the biggest market news. - The Planner lists the results of the companies you hold or watch, dividends coming to you (or owed on shares sold short), a margin call to meet, orders about to lapse, and your bonds' payments and their ends. # A margin account - With 'Margin trading' on, open one on the Portfolio tab's Your account page with Open a margin account, paying in {mkt_margin_open} or more; Pay in and Take out move cash in and out of it. It can borrow against your shares, and sell short the shares of a company that can be borrowed: not a small company, a new listing, one in distress, one under a bid or a rival's holding. - When you buy, {mkt_initial} of everything held must be your own money. If what you own falls under {mkt_maintenance_long} of what you hold ({mkt_maintenance_short} of what you owe, {mkt_risky_extra} more for a risky company) at the close, the broker makes a margin call: meet it by the next close, or the broker sells. Under {mkt_forced} of that the broker sells at once, and what is still owed is taken from your cash. - What is borrowed costs the bank rate and {mkt_margin_rate} a year. Borrowing shares costs {mkt_borrow_least} to {mkt_borrow_most} a year of their worth, and a short pays the dividends. With 'Margin trading' off, an open account can only be wound down. # Bonds - On the Bonds tab you can lend your cash for a fixed term to the city's Treasury, to the city itself or, as a deposit, to one of the city's three largest banks. Each pays interest every month or every quarter (a three-month Treasury bond once, at its end) and repays what you put in at the end of its term. - A bond is bought while the market trades, at 100 for each 100 it repays, with no commission: from {bond_least} up to the larger of {bond_most} and {bond_most_share} of what you are worth (the game's own figure with what you hold on the market), {bond_most_cap} at most; with 'Worked orders and larger bond purchases' off, up to {bond_most}. You can hold {bond_holdings} at once, {bond_holdings_large} with that option on. Its rate is fixed when you buy it: the bank rate with half of its next decision counts for a short term and the long run for a long one (over about {bond_short_years} years), with {bond_term_premium} more for each year of its term, {bond_term_premium_most} at most. A city bond pays {bond_city_spread} more than the Treasury's, a deposit {bond_deposit_under} less, and {bond_deposit_point} more at a bank whose loans are a point dearer. - Tax is withheld from its interest as from a dividend. Of what is left you choose how much goes back into the same bond at the day's price: none, a quarter, half, three quarters or all of it. The rest is paid into your cash, a transaction of its own each time, with a notification that adds what the bond has paid so far while 'A bond's interest so far' is on. The last payment is paid out in full, with what the bond repays. - A bond or a deposit can be set to roll over: at its end it is bought again at once, the same kind and term at that day's rate, with what it repays and the last payment's share you put back, and so on until you change it. Buy the ladder spreads one sum evenly over the Treasury's {bond_ladder_terms} terms in one go, a bond of each, so that one comes to its end after each term; each part can roll over too. - Sold before its end, a bond brings every payment still to come and what it repays, discounted at today's rate for what is left of its term: less when rates have risen, more when they have fallen, and {bond_sell_treasury} less for a Treasury bond, {bond_sell_city} for a city bond. A deposit cannot be sold: Close it repays what is in it less {bond_penalty_months} months' interest. - With 'Bonds and deposits' off none can be bought and none rolls over; those you hold still pay, end and can be sold. In a Going Public session your bonds are yours alone, and your worked orders and dividends put back are your own orders. # Options - Under 'The stock market' on the options page, all on unless you change them: 'The city's stock market' (off, the Stocks app leaves your phone and what you hold waits in the save), 'Margin trading', 'Bonds and deposits', 'Worked orders and larger bond purchases' and 'Dividends put back into the same shares' (switched off, what is open of it is cancelled; what it bought or sold is kept), the two notifications, and 'The most of a company you may hold'. # What to expect - Prices are a fair bet. Over the years holding the market returns about what its risk is paid, with losing years and the odd crash. In the mod's own tests no rule of thumb beat holding by more than its risk. - Bonds return about the city's rates: less than shares over the years, and far steadier. A property trust is a share like any other: its frequent payments are part of what its price is worth, not money on top of it. - The save tools sell everything, your bonds included, at today's price before the mod is removed.

reallife_guide_ledger_about: The city's morning paper as a real newspaper: delivered to your door if you subscribe, bought at a kiosk near your home, or read on your phone with Newsstand.
reallife_guide_ledger: # The paper - The City Ledger is the city's morning paper, written every day from what happened: the street (accidents, crime, arrests, fires), the courts, City Hall (elections and the council's policies), the economy (the bank rate, prices, shortages), business (your own shops and bank, strikes, the rival tycoons), the stock market (the index, the risers and fallers, results, dividends, listings, bids and failures), the weather, what's on, people you know and the city's small news. - It comes out at {ledger_delivery}. In print, only a copy can be read: one left at your home, or one bought at a kiosk. Online, it is read on your phone with Newsstand, by subscription. - A few pages open as a front page of its own in the paper's look: the city's rich list (see 'Rival tycoons') and, under Permadeath, a front page in memory. # Delivered to your door - Call the contact City Ledger on your phone to have it delivered: {ledger_week} for {ledger_days} mornings, paid a week at a time, the first week when you subscribe. It needs a home to be left at. The first paper comes the next morning, or this morning if the round has not been yet. - Each morning the paper lies on the floor just inside your front door, and a notification says it has come. Point at it and click to read it. - Call again to cancel: the paper still comes until the last day you paid for, and nothing more is charged. Call before that day to keep it coming, with nothing to pay until its next week. A week that cannot be paid stops the delivery. A morning the round cannot come (no home, the paper switched off) is never charged: the days you paid for wait. The Calendar app shows each week's payment, and the last paper of a cancelled one. # At a kiosk - {ledger_kiosks} newspaper kiosks stand on the pavement within {ledger_far} m of your home: on the city map they are Newspaper kiosks, with the building behind each lit. They are open from {ledger_open} to {ledger_close}. - At the counter the game's panel sells today's paper for {ledger_copy} on {key_interact} or a click (Buy the paper), and opens it. A copy you bought can be read again there (Read it), and at home. A paper that cannot be opened is never charged. # On your phone: Newsstand - Newsstand is an app on your phone. It opens in the full-screen phone like the other apps: the Titles tab lists the papers, and the Reading tab shows the one you pick as one column of newsprint. Scroll it with the mouse wheel, or drag it. - Four titles, each written every morning from the same news as the printed paper, each with its own pages: The City Ledger online, {ledger_online_ledger} a week (all of it, with every share price); The Exchange Gazette, {ledger_online_exchange} (the markets, the economy and business in full, with every share price); The Street Sheet, {ledger_online_street} (crime, accidents, the courts and City Hall); The Weekend Review, {ledger_online_review} (what's on, the city after dark and its people). The Newsstand Pass has all four for {ledger_online_pass} a week; your own titles' subscriptions then stop at their last paid day. - Subscribe and Cancel in the app, and Take it up again before a cancelled one ends. A week is paid at a time, the first when you subscribe, and today's edition comes at once. A cancelled subscription runs to the last day paid for. Each charge is a line of its own in the Finance app, and the Planner shows the morning each subscription renews or ends. - Subscribing needs a working internet connection at one of your homes: buy one in the Utilities app, on its Internet tab (Open Utilities takes you there). The new editions come over it at {ledger_delivery}. While it is down or cut nothing new comes and nothing is charged: the days you paid for wait until it is back. What has come can be read anywhere, connected or not. - The editions of the last {ledger_online_days} mornings can be opened again on the Reading tab, and the City Ledger online can be opened as The printed page. A notification each morning names the papers that came, after you wake if you slept through it. - With 'Power, water and internet bills' off on the options page, a home of your own counts as connected. # The page - Front page: the lead story under its headline, the rest of the news in columns, and a box down the side with the markets, the weather and what is inside. On a quiet day the city index's last sessions are drawn under the columns. - Markets: the market's stories, the city index over its last {ledger_chart} sessions, every sector, the risers, the fallers and the most traded. - Share prices: every listed company's close and its move on the day, by sector, with marks for a bid, a dividend, a new listing and a split. - The paper reports the market's last close and the news already out: what it prints is what anybody could know that morning. # Options - Under the City Ledger on the options page, all on unless you change them: 'The City Ledger morning paper' (off, there is no paper at all, Newsstand included), 'Newspaper kiosks near your home' (off, there are no kiosks), 'Online papers on your phone (Newsstand)' and 'A notification when the morning's papers come'.

reallife_changes_003_1: A stock market of its own: some 136 of the city's companies in a new Stocks app, with candle charts, the usual analysis tools, each company's figures and every usual kind of order, priced from their business and moved by everything in the city. The City Ledger is now a real newspaper: subscribe on the phone to have it left at your door each morning, or buy a copy at a kiosk near your home. At bus stops beside parking the buses now have a zone of their own: the parking there is cut back, bins and barricades in the road are cleared, and the bus pulls in to the kerb. The bus is the mod's own city bus, with doors that open at the stop, lamps and indicators, and the stop's countdown now matches when it pulls in. With mouse look you can look up past the horizon to the tops of the buildings, on foot and in the car. The mod's apps no longer go missing from the phone after a bank's app changes, and the top bar of the phone's full screen shares them out evenly over its pages, with the page dots level with the icons. The mod's clothes are in the game's own clothes screen: at home your wardrobe's Change clothes has what you bought, and the rack in a clothing store opens the same screen as a shop, with the prices and a Buy button.

reallife_changes_003_2: The mod's bus and its other props no longer show the road's markings through them as if they were glass, and a bus stop's painted box now covers where the bus stands, some 24 m, not the whole zone. You can switch off the notifications about accidents near you, and the waypoint to them, on the options page: the accidents still happen, without the messages and their sound, or without the marker. A business that is closed for want of power, water or an internet connection now tells you why and what opens it again (a bought building's temporary supply runs out after three days unless you apply at the utilities office).

reallife_guide_multiplayer: Going Public, a mod of the Steam Workshop, lets several players share one city. Here and now: {session}. The city's economy, government and stock market: {city}. On the options page, Troubleshooting, Going Public (multiplayer) has two buttons that say this again in a notice. # The city is the host's - The city's economy is one for every player: the host's bank rate and the central bank's decisions, prices and inflation, the good and bad times, each district's income and the supply of goods. Prices, loans and footfall in every player's game follow it. - So is its government: the mayor, the council, the policies in force and on their way, the elections with their candidates, polls and count, approval, petitions and the building sites. - And its stock market: one market, the host's, with the same prices to the cent on every screen. Each player's shares, orders and account stay their own. The host's listed company is on it for everyone; a guest's own listed company is set aside until they play alone ('Your company on the market'). - One City Ledger, printed by the host with every player's news in it, and one Flare feed. Your posts and pictures go to everyone if you share them in Flare's options. - The city's faults, the calendar of street events and the spells of weather are the host's too, and everyone has the same seasons, snow and rain. - A guest's game runs none of it alone: it follows the host's, which comes every few seconds. What a guest does counts in the host's city: a ballot is counted in the host's election, a donation, an endorsement, leaflets or a rally move its polls, and so do a petition, a signature, a complaint or a report about a site; every trade moves the one market. - The city's notices (a campaign, a policy, a result) reach every player. - A guest who leaves, or whose host has gone, keeps the city as it last was, and it carries on from there in their own game. - This needs the same version of this mod for every player. With another version a guest is told so, and their city stays their own. # Each player's own - Every player plays their own save, and this mod's part of it is theirs: money, businesses, home, family, friends, jobs, the record, the Planner. What it does there happens for that player alone. - Street life, scenes, conversations, the camera, photo mode, the sounds and the phone's apps are each player's own, on their own screen. The people on the pavement that one player sees are not on the others' screens, and another player is never a passer-by you talk to. - Another player's business, home or staff is theirs: this mod never charges you for it, never closes it and never counts it as yours. When you close a business of yours, or a fire closes it, the others see it closed. - You may drive another player's car. This mod never tows it, impounds it or bills you for it. # The clock is everyone's - Nothing of this mod pauses the clock, skips it or speeds it in a session. Time passes faster only by a vote of every player, from an activity the game's own panel shows: a bed, a bench, the rest of a shift. - What would have passed time takes none: custody and prison are served at once, and a ride behind a black screen, a visit to the garage, an outing indoors and the family's occasions are over at once. A bus you ride in real time has no fast forward, and an interview takes its own time behind the black screen. The record, the fines and the court's order stand as they would. - Photo mode does not pause, and neither does arranging cars in your showroom: the city and the clock go on around you. - Holidays are not booked, a ticket you hold waits, and a trip already under way is cut short. In a hotel room you cannot sleep, rest or go for a walk while time passes. # Classes and desks - Going Public hides the game's activity panel and starts the activity for you. A study desk with nothing to start opens nothing and says why in a notice. - At the school a class is joined with {key_interact} where you stand, as the desks' clicks are Going Public's. At the university a classroom door opens the class's own panel. # A guest's traffic - Near the host, a guest's traffic is the host's cars. Nothing of this mod takes a car from it there: traffic accidents and the emergency response, tow trucks, police chases and patrols, buses, City Cabs, fires, street events, the driving test and the drivers you can watch go wrong happen for the host only. The weather does not slow a guest's traffic either. - A franchised shop a guest opens is in their books only; the host's opens in the city. # Waits, or is not offered, while a session is on - Selling a business: what is listed and offered waits, untouched. - An agreed sale of a building completes the first day you play alone. - Hiring out your cars: cars already out come back as usual. - The rivals rest: nothing of theirs grows or moves, and they go on when you play alone. - Every future is settled in cash: nothing is delivered to a warehouse or factory. - A contact's tip on a building for sale does not lower what its seller takes. - Standing for office and a car for your partner are not offered, and Permadeath is off. # Going Public's add-ons - Extras, the French translation and Friend Trade add to Going Public's own menus, map and trades, and need nothing of this mod.
reallife_changes_003_7: Living with Going Public, the multiplayer mod: in one of its sessions this mod passes no time of its own (custody, prison, rides and outings take none, and photo mode does not pause), never treats another player's business or home as yours, and leaves what takes cars out of the traffic to the host. Holidays, nights in a hotel, selling a business or a building and hiring out cars wait until you play alone. A notice says so once, the options that do nothing in a session are greyed with the reason, and the Guide has a page on it.

reallife_guide_flare: # Flare - Flare is an app on the phone, in the dock at first. Its rail has Home (For you, Following), Explore (Trending, Accounts), Notifications, Messages, Business and Profile (Posts, Replies, Pictures), and the Post button. - Your account starts with the people you have met and {flare_start_extra} more followers. - The button on Flare's top bar switches its look at once: it says 'Dark' while Flare is light and 'Light' while it is dark. The choice is kept. It is the same setting as 'Flare's look' on the options page, where 'Follows the phone' makes Flare dark from {flare_dark_from} to {flare_dark_until}. # Posting - Post opens New post. Under "What is it about?" choose Now (a post in your own words), A moment (something that happened to you; shown while one is waiting), Report, Review or Announce (with a business of yours). - A moment is made by what you really did: a picture or a selfie you saved, an outing that went to its end, a promotion or a rung up your profession, graduation day, a business opened or its best day yet, a striking interior in the paper, a vote, an endorsement, a campaign event, a good turn, an arrest, the results of a company you hold, a crime or a crash in the city to speak about, an answer to a scandal. Each waits {flare_draft_days} days, {flare_drafts_most} at most, and Home says how many are waiting. - Write up to {flare_text_most} characters and add up to {flare_tags_most} tags. For a picture, the camera button opens the phone's Camera (with the Camera off it takes the screen as it is), the selfie button opens its selfie view, and the third button picks your latest photo. The Gallery's To Flare button does the same from a photo you took. - Pick a tone: Cheerful, Proud, Honest or Cheeky. The one that suits what happened is chosen first. A tone that suits it brings more followers; the wrong one (cheerful about an arrest) goes badly and costs followers and reputation, and if enough people saw it, a pile-on follows and the City Ledger hears of it. An arrest or an answer to a scandal suits only Honest. - Post as often as you like. Your first {flare_posts_counted} posts of a day (of any kind but reports and replies) grow your account; more are seen, liked and answered, and leave your followers and reputation as they are, and New post says so. The same kind of post again within {flare_repeat_days} days brings less. # Followers - Followers grow ever more slowly as the account grows. The tiers: Local from {flare_local}, Known from {flare_known}, Influencer from {flare_influencer}, Celebrity from {flare_celebrity}. - After {flare_silent_days} days without a post, followers drift away a little each day. Replies and reports do not count as posts for this. - A post can go viral, once in {flare_viral_gap} days at most and with a chance of {flare_viral_most}% at best. - Your reputation on Flare moves a little each day towards what the city thinks of you. # What a post does - A post about one of your businesses (its opening, a record day, a picture taken inside) brings it more customers for {flare_buzz_days} days: more for a post many people see, up to {flare_buzz_most}% from Flare in all. A post that went badly adds nothing. - From {flare_sponsored_from} followers the Company app's Marketing tab offers a sponsored post on Flare. It is priced by your followers and your reputation there, and measured like any other campaign. - A viral post about a business gets the city talking about one of its products, once in {flare_hype_gap} days at most, and a viral day is in the next City Ledger. - A friend you tag is a little closer for it; a selfie taken with them on an outing counts twice, and tagging your partner pleases them more. Tagging somebody in a post that goes badly costs a little trust. - When a brand of yours has a scandal, a doubted account makes the talk worse. An honest answer posted within {flare_draft_days} days wins part of the loss back. - From Local on, an arrest trends: {flare_arrest_share}% of your followers go. A picture posted while you are wanted has the police watching more closely for the rest of the day. - Your following adds to your word when you endorse a candidate, at most as much as two businesses. A post about a campaign event adds to your campaign, or as a councillor to your approval. - If the boss of your rota job follows you, a moment posted during a rota shift is a complaint at your next review, once a day at most. Off shift, a boss who follows you likes your posts. # Friends - With the social life on, friends follow you from acquaintance on. They like and answer your posts by what they care about, and post their own. # The rest of the city - Now and then somebody you have still to meet answers one of your posts and you swap numbers: a contact met online. A bigger account meets a few more a month. - Tag somebody you could fall for while you are with a partner, and your partner reads it by their nature: proud, cool or jealous. Never posting your partner for {flare_never_days} days while you post others, they mind it. A friend whose texts you leave waiting minds seeing you post all day. - Listed companies post their results in the feed. You can post about the results of a company you hold shares in; from Known on your post says you hold them. Selling those shares within {flare_abuse_days} days of such a post going viral is market abuse, and a case goes to court. - A viral post about one of your businesses gives its trade a lift on the stock market, and a brand's scandal the other way. - The City Ledger has its own account: each morning's headlines, one line each. The full pieces are in the paper. - After a crime or a crash in the city you can post about safety or the roads, which raises it in the council a little. The feed's mood about how the city is run pulls on the mayor's approval, a point a day at most. - As a Celebrity, a lawyer asks {flare_fame_fee}% more of you, and your day in court is in the paper. # Influencers - The city has influencers from the first day, each with a niche, a home district, followers, engagement, reliability, a price and a manner. They post every day: their niche, the day's news, a visit to one of your businesses in their district (a little more custom for {flare_buzz_days} days), a rival who paid them, a candidate. - Each month some grow, some fade or stop, a few become stars (from {flare_star_from} followers), and some are caught in a scandal, which the City Ledger reports. A friend or one of your staff may take it up. The city starts with {flare_cast_start} and settles at about {flare_cast_level} at a time. - A star may turn out to be somebody you have still to meet: a friend will introduce you. - To hire, open Business and press Hire an influencer on a business's card (an influencer's profile has the button too). Choose one post, a series of {flare_series_days} days, an ambassador for {flare_ambassador_days} days, a plan of two or three influencers, a launch for a business in its first fortnight, or a giveaway (it costs stock, like a discount day). The hire shows the cost and about how many more customers. It needs Marketing campaigns of Running a business on. - Each hire is a campaign of the Company app: paid when booked, the same report, the same cap, a cost you can deduct. Their niche and district decide how well it lands. A business has one campaign at a time, of any kind: if one is running or booked, from the Company app or on Flare, the hire says which and until when. Business lists the company's campaigns beside your deals. - A deal's posts begin the day after you hire and are spread over its days, marked as a paid partnership. Each influencer in it posts once for a single post, {flare_series_posts} times in a series, {flare_ambassador_posts} for an ambassador, {flare_plan_posts} in a plan, {flare_launch_posts} in a launch and {flare_giveaway_posts} in a giveaway, and the deal is priced for just those posts. They are in the feed among the newest posts, and the deal's row says how many have come. You are only told when they post if you follow them. - A flaky influencer may post a day late or off message; an edgy one can backfire. If one you hired has a scandal, the talk turns against your business and its brand, and End the deal stops it. Ending a deal ends its campaign too, so the business is free again by the next day. # Following and notifications - A new game follows nobody. Explore and then Accounts lists the official accounts, the players in a session, the influencers, brands, candidates and the city's people; open one and press Follow. Home and then Following shows your friends', the players' and the followed accounts' posts. - Of the accounts you follow, influencers, brands, candidates, listed companies and the City Ledger send one notification a day at most, from 08:00, however many of them posted. - The app's badge counts what you have not read (likes, replies, shares, answers to your reports, reviews of your businesses, messages) and the moments waiting. - What needs you sends a notification, one a day at most of these: a viral post, a pile-on, a poor review of your business, a scandal of an influencer you hired. Answers to your reports and invitations have their own. The Flare notifications option switches them off. # The living city - The feed is the city's own: its {flare_citizens} people post about the weather, the news, prices, the street's events and the election; the City Office, the police, the transit company, the utilities office and the bank post as things happen; businesses post their offers; your rivals post about their latest moves. How busy it is is an option. Trending shows the day's tags. - Likes, replies and shares come in over the next hours from people with names: your partner, friends, staff and boss among them. - Under the posts of the city's people, the accounts, the businesses and the influencers, comments come in over the hours. With RLO Texts on, every one of them is written out by its model, up to {flare_comments_most} under a post, and only past that does the thread say how many more replied. Without it the thread shows only how many replied. # Messages and invitations - People of the city write to you now and then (a fan after a viral post, somebody asking about the job you announced, an influencer, a chat after a post of yours), and answer your messages. The city's people, influencers and official accounts have a Message button on their profile. - Invite somebody out in a message, for a coffee, a meal, drinks, the cinema, a walk or a workout, and the game decides: yes, maybe or no. A yes names a place and a time and books the outing as a call would. Somebody you have never met says yes only after {flare_invite_chats} messages of theirs, or with a standing of {flare_invite_standing}, and then joins People as met online, with the face they have on Flare. Somebody seeing someone else, or who thinks poorly of you, says no; late at night or with a plan already on, maybe. An influencer always says maybe. # Reports and the City Office - Report a broken road, a street light out, crime, litter, an unsafe place, a business (stand inside it), the buses or the power or water, as often as you like. Flare must know your district: outdoors is best. The City Office or the right account answers within {flare_reply_most_hours} hours. The same report again the same day joins the case already filed, and the first {flare_reports_day} reports of a day weigh in the council. - A road or a street light gets a crew: real works near you, with the days they take ({flare_crews_works} crews a week), while the council feature is on. Crime brings police patrols to the district for {flare_patrol_days} days ({flare_crews_patrol} a week); litter a cleaning round for {flare_cleanup_days} days ({flare_crews_cleanup} a week); a business an inspection that turns the talk against it for {flare_inspection_days} days ({flare_crews_inspection} a week). An unsafe place near a building site gets an inspector, otherwise a patrol. The buses and the power or water get an answer only. - When the crews are busy the complaint waits. {flare_tally} complaints of one kind in one district in a week with nothing done reach the City Ledger, and the mayor's approval falls. - With City faults on, the City Office checks each report against the city's real faults first (see the City faults page): a real one gets a crew, a report of nothing is answered so and costs {flare_false_cost} points of your Flare reputation, and the city's people report only real faults. - Call on an account in a post names an official account, a brand or a player, and that account answers. # Reviews and announcements - A review gives a business one to five stars and moves its customers for {flare_review_days} days, more for a review many people saw. You cannot review your own. Answer a poor review of yours politely (not cheeky) to win a little back. Your first review of a business each day moves it, and your first announcement of each kind; more that day only show in the feed. - Announce a sale, new hours, an event, a job or something new at your business, also from Announce on its card. An event is an invitation others can say they are going to, and it draws custom until its day. # Pictures - Every account has a picture beside its name: people show their faces, drawn once by the game's own portrait camera from the look they have in the street (the initials stand in until then); a business or a brand its logo; the city's offices, the City Ledger, listed companies, candidates and the rival tycoons an emblem. You show your latest selfie posted on Flare, or your character's portrait. - Some of the city's posts carry a photo. While you are out, on foot or driving, Flare quietly photographs the streets, shop fronts, parks, sights and street events you pass, never indoors, in each district by day, at dusk and at night, dry or in the rain. A post shows one that fits it, or none. # Going Public - In a session the city has one feed and one City Ledger. Your posts and pictures go to everyone if you share them (the options), pictures as small copies of at most {flare_picture_kb} KB, {flare_pictures_day} a day. Past that your posts still go, without their pictures, and you are told once. Each player's game takes its own photos and draws its own faces. - What other players type is filtered (Steam's own filter, or the mod's word list), and you can mute or hide a player. A review of another player's business changes their customers on their own game only.

reallife_changes_003_9: Flare, a social media app on the phone: post your pictures, selfies, outings, promotions, new shops, votes and good turns, gain followers, and see your friends like and answer. A post about your shop brings customers, a sponsored post is a new campaign in the Company app, and a viral moment reaches the City Ledger, the brands, the election, the police and your boss. The city has influencers of its own who post about real places and events, grow, fade and have scandals; hire them for a post, a series, an ambassador deal, a plan, a launch or a giveaway, and follow the accounts you want to hear from. People you have still to meet may answer a post, your partner reads your posts, the stock market and the City Ledger post too, and the five newest pictures show in their posts.
reallife_changes_004_0: In a Going Public session the city is one city for every player, the host's: its economy (the bank rate, prices, the good and bad times, the districts, supply), its government (the mayor, the council, policies, elections, petitions and the building sites) and its stock market, with the same prices on every screen. A guest's vote, donation, petition, complaint or trade counts in the host's city, a guest who leaves carries on from the city as it was, and each player's money, shares and businesses stay their own.

reallife_guide_permadeath_about: An ending you can choose: with it on, your character can die for good after a warning, and the City Ledger prints their obituary.
reallife_guide_permadeath: # What it is - Off unless you switch it on, and kept with each save: switching it on in one save does not touch another, and no preset sets it. Switched on in the main menu, it applies to the next new game you start. - With it on, your character can die for good. Every danger warns you first, and nothing can happen during the game's tutorial, one of its missions or a Going Public session. - Switching it on asks you first. You can switch it off again at any time while your character lives. # What can end a life - A crash in your own car at an impact of {pd_crash_from} km/h or more. The first is a near miss: hospital, and a notice that says the next one could be fatal. After that such a crash is fatal {pd_crash_least} of the time at {pd_crash_from} km/h, rising to {pd_crash_most} from {pd_crash_worst} km/h. - Being hit on foot by a vehicle at {pd_struck_from} km/h or more. The first time is a near miss. After that it is fatal {pd_struck_least} of the time at {pd_struck_from} km/h, rising to {pd_struck_most} from {pd_struck_worst} km/h. - Refusing a mugger: the mugger may run off, or may hurt you. With Permadeath on, the mugger's demand says what refusing can cost; the first time you are hurt is a near miss, and after that one hurt in {pd_mug_one_in} is fatal. - The private lender's men, over a debt long past its day: the first beating is a near miss, and after that one in {pd_assault_one_in} is fatal. Paying the debt ends it. - A flu left untreated: after {pd_ill_first} days it gets worse and no longer clears up by itself, with a warning. More warnings follow after {pd_ill_second} and {pd_ill_last} days, and from {pd_ill_fatal} days untreated it is fatal about {pd_ill_day} of the time over each further day. Medicine from a doctor or a stay in hospital ends the danger. - Going without food: after {pd_starve_first} hours with your hunger bar empty you feel weak with hunger, with a warning and a low mood. After {pd_starve_second} hours you feel faint and tire faster, and after {pd_starve_last} hours you are starving. From {pd_starve_fatal} hours without food it is fatal about {pd_starve_day} of the time over each further day, never while you sleep, in hospital or in the middle of something. Eating anything ends the danger, and a stay in hospital fills you up. - Nothing else: life events, crimes you only watch, fires and other people's accidents never end your life. - A danger whose own option is off cannot happen: with Your crashes cost money and can injure you off there is no danger in your car, with Traffic can knock you down on foot off none on foot, and with Illness and the doctor off no flu. # When it happens - The screen fades and the game is saved at once with the death in it, so quitting cannot undo it. The City Ledger then prints a front page in memory: the name, the age, how they died, the career and the best qualification, the businesses founded and still open, the estate, the staff and the properties, family and friends, any record, the Flare followers, the elections voted in, the time in the city and who mourns them. - Putting the paper down goes back to the main menu. The save's files are kept: opening that save again shows the obituary and goes back to the menu. An older save of the same character, from a time Permadeath was on in it, ends the same way on this computer. - Once a character has died, switching Permadeath off cannot bring them back. # In a Going Public session - Permadeath is off while a session is on, hosted or joined: another player's world is never ended. It is on again when you play alone.

reallife_guide_standing:
# Standing
- Standing is what the city knows and thinks of you, in three parts: your wealth, your recognition (how many people know you) and your reputation (what they think of you). See it on the Standing page: the Finance app's Overview has a button for it.
- A rich owner nobody has heard of, a popular local owner and a famous tycoon with a poor name are all possible.
# Wealth and recognition
- Wealth comes from what you are worth, a week's income from your businesses and lettings, and the businesses you run. Every tenfold counts about the same.
- Recognition is {standing_wealth_share}% of your wealth, your followers on Flare (up to {standing_followers_most} points), what the papers and the television made of you (up to {standing_press_most} points, slowly forgotten) and your brand's name. Each business adds {standing_shop_known} points in its own district.
- The levels: Known locally from {standing_local}, Known from {standing_known}, Prominent from {standing_prominent}, Famous from {standing_famous}.
# Reputation
- Four parts, each from 0 to 100 and starting at 50. Customers: their satisfaction and their view of your prices. Workers: your staff's standing in the Company app, strikes and those who stand low. Neighbourhoods: each district counts {standing_job_points} points for each job you bring there (up to {standing_job_most}) and loses {standing_raised_points} for each home you let above the market's rent (up to {standing_raised_most}). Integrity: only what you do.
- The first three move towards what is read each day, {standing_drift_most} points a day at most. What you do moves a part by {standing_day_most} points a day at most, either way. Integrity forgets a point every {standing_forget_days} days towards 50.
- Good deeds, complaints answered, praise shared, inspections passed and strikes settled raise it; complaints ignored, failed inspections and strikes refused lower it.
# The street, your shops and your staff
- Where you are known by {standing_street_from} or more, people in the street sometimes know you: a look, a greeting, a word about your money, praise, or a complaint about the rents where you raised them. {standing_street_most} a day at most.
- Customers in your own shops may know you. Your staff are proud to see you when your workers' reputation is {standing_proud_from} or more and nervous under {standing_nervous_under}: their standing moves a point either way, in {standing_visits_most} businesses a day at most.
- All of this is one notice a day at most.
# The press
- From a recognition of {standing_reporter_from}, a reporter of the City Ledger may come up to you in the street, once in {standing_reporter_gap} days at most. Answer, and they ask two questions: how you got here or what comes next, then a hard one about your weakest part, or a promise. From {standing_photo_from} a photographer may take your picture.
- From {standing_magazine_from} Avenue magazine may ask you for an interview, and from {standing_show_from} the night show Late Lights may ask you on, {standing_invite_gap} days apart at most. Accept within {standing_answer_days} days on the Standing page; it goes in your Planner. The show is at {standing_show_hour}, the magazine at {standing_magazine_hour}: be free at the hour, not driving and not busy. Missing one is noticed.
- Each answer moves your recognition and a part of your reputation. Honest answers to hard questions help your integrity; brushing them off makes more noise and costs it. The show counts most.
- A promise is judged {standing_promise_days} days on, or as soon as you keep it: kept, integrity +{standing_kept}; broken, -{standing_broken}. The papers say which.
- From {standing_story_from} the City Ledger writes about you: a second, fifth, tenth or twentieth business, your first and fifth building, criticism over your staff's conditions or your customers' patience, the rents in a district, praise for the jobs you bring. One piece a day at most.
# What it does to business
- Your customers' reputation and each district's opinion bring a business more customers or fewer, as far as the district knows you: {standing_footfall_most}% at most either way.
- A poor name with customers brings more complaints and less praise. Poor integrity brings more inspections and audits, and so does being well known.
- A good name as an employer helps a newcomer settle in and keeps rivals from your staff; a poor one does the opposite.
# Walking on
- If you come up to an accident or a crime with a victim and walk on without helping while others are near, your integrity drops {standing_refused}. It may be in the paper, which costs {standing_reported} more; the better known you are, the likelier.
# Connections and power
- From a recognition and a wealth of {standing_request_from}, the city asks something of you now and then, {standing_request_gap} days apart at most: sponsor a street party or pay for a corner to be done up ({standing_sponsor_boost}% more customers in the district for a few days), give to charity, save a struggling shop, answer a public complaint, or another owner's joint promotion ({standing_partner_boost}% more customers at one business for {standing_partner_days} days). Each costs a share of a week's income. Answer within {standing_request_days} days on the Standing page; a complaint left unanswered costs you.
- From a wealth of {standing_investors_wealth} and a recognition of {standing_investors_from} you may be invited to an evening with investors, and from {standing_reception_from} to a reception at City Hall. Accept them as you would the show. There you can talk business (another owner may offer a partnership), have a word with the council's people (your next push on the council counts more) and meet new people, who become contacts.
- With an influence of {standing_influence_from} or more (your recognition and your reputation together), the Standing page lists the changes the council could make for business. Push for one with a lobbyist's fee: rival businesses back the other side, your chance is between {standing_lobby_least}% and {standing_lobby_most}%, the council decides in {standing_lobby_days} days, and you can push again after {standing_lobby_rest} days.
# Bribes
- With its option on, an official on the Business desk may offer to make an inspection or a licence a formality for cash, {standing_bribe_offer}% of the time. A bribe costs {standing_bribe_integrity} integrity at once. From {standing_surface_after} days on it may come out: a court case for bribery and a scandal of {standing_scandal_days} days, with {standing_scandal_footfall}% fewer customers everywhere, more inspections, staff readier to leave and partnerships called off.

reallife_fame_part_about_0: What your customers make of your businesses: their satisfaction counts most, and their view of your prices the rest. It moves a little each day towards where their figures put it. Answering complaints, sharing praise and passing inspections help.
reallife_fame_part_about_1: What it is like to work for you: your staff's standing in the Company app, less for those who stand low and for a strike. Raises, settled strikes and visits when your staff are proud help; refused raises and walkouts hurt.
reallife_fame_part_about_2: What each district thinks of you: the jobs you bring raise it, homes you let above the market's rent lower it. This is the average of the districts where you have a business or let a home.
reallife_fame_part_about_3: Moved only by what you do: good deeds, kept promises and gifts to charity raise it; bribes, broken promises and walking past somebody who needs help in front of others lower it. It forgets a point a week towards 50.

reallife_guide_trouble_empire: # With Empire Motors - Empire Motors, a car dealership mod of the Steam Workshop, works beside this mod, which now has one of its own, the Car Showroom. Both can run in one city: each kind keeps its own cars, customers and app. - Its dealership is one of your businesses here too. Its car sales, finance payments and warranty premiums are its takings in the game's statement, and what its cars cost to buy, inspect, recondition and service, and its supplies and campaigns, are its costs. So the Company app, brands, business pressure, the price of a sale, business loans and Flare see what it really makes, and the game's yearly tax counts its takings and deducts those costs as it does a shop's goods. This needs Money and credit switched on. Empire Motors brings it its customers itself, so the Company app's campaigns and a brand's footfall do not reach it. - The cars of its stock are the dealership's, not yours to run: they have no Garage page and no service, insurance or registration of this mod's, are never taken for a car bought on car finance, and cannot go on hire or into the custom shop. Sell the stock in Empire Motors before you sell the dealership on the Sell tab of the Services app. - In a car, V is still this mod's camera key. While it is V, Empire Motors' own view from the driver's seat, which reads the same key, is kept off, so the chase camera stays yours. To use that view, give this mod's camera key another key in the options; the chase camera then stands aside while that view is on. Empire Motors also acts on F6, F7, F9 and F12 by itself: the options page says so beside any of this mod's keys that are the same, so that you can move them. - Its Mustang GT and BMW G82 add-ons have figures of their own in car tuning: sports cars of 4.5 and 4.0 seconds to 100 km/h, 250 km/h at most.
reallife_co_push_empire: Empire Motors brings this dealership its customers itself, so a campaign of this app's would change nothing here. None can be booked: its own campaigns are in its app.
reallife_brand_member_empire: Empire Motors brings this dealership its customers itself, so the brand cannot bring it more. Its standards still count in the brand's.
reallife_changes_004_3: Empire Motors, the car dealership mod of the Steam Workshop, works beside this mod. Its dealerships are businesses like any other here: their car sales and costs are in the game's statement, so the Company app, brands, the price of a sale and business loans see what they make, and the game's tax counts their margin. The cars of their stock are left to the dealership (no Garage page, records, car finance, hire or custom shop for them), a dealership with stock is not sold, and the Company app sells no campaign for it, as Empire Motors brings its customers itself. In a car, V is left to its view from the driver's seat, its other keys are named beside this mod's on the options page, and its Mustang GT and BMW G82 add-ons have their own figures in car tuning.
reallife_changes_004_4: Standing: the city reacts to your success. Your wealth, how well you are known and what people think of you as an owner (customers, workers, neighbourhoods, integrity) are on a new page of the Finance app, with what moves each. People in the street, customers in your shops and your staff take notice of you. Reporters stop you in the street, the night show and a magazine invite you, your promises are remembered, and the City Ledger writes about your rise. Your name brings customers or costs them, and walking past somebody who needs help is seen. The city asks you to sponsor events, give to charity, save a shop or answer a complaint; evenings with investors and receptions at City Hall bring new people and partnerships; you can lobby the council; and an official may offer to make an inspection a formality for a bribe, which can come out later.
reallife_changes_004_5: Permadeath, an ending you can choose: off unless you switch it on, and kept with each save. With it on, your character can die for good, but only after a warning: a crash at very high speed, being hit by fast traffic on foot, a mugging refused, the private lender's men or a flu left untreated past three warnings. The game is saved at once, the City Ledger prints a front page in memory with their life's story, and the save can be opened again to read it but never played. It is off in a Going Public session and during the game's tutorial and missions.

reallife_guide_tech_people: # Who counts - Every employee whose main skill is programmer, graphic designer, lawyer, HR manager or headhunter, and customer service staff at an office. Shop staff keep the game's own hiring. - The game's skill is shown as a per cent in its own staff list. Here it is the main skill, and each role adds two skills of its own, also 0% to 100%. - The Open Roles app lists your team. Pick someone for their file, their career and their contract. # Roles {talent_roles} - A role marked as on the payroll has no job in the game: those people are not drawn in the building, are paid by the hour each working day and count at the business they work for. # Levels {talent_levels} # Learning - Each hour of work adds to both of a role's skills, less as they near 100%. - A senior or above at the same business mentors up to {talent_mentees} juniors or mids of the same family: they learn {talent_mentor} faster and their game skill grows a little too. - A course adds up to {talent_course_gain} points to one skill over {talent_course_days} days, outside working hours. It is paid by the business. - An exam gives a certificate. At the score it needs the pass chance is {talent_exam_pass}, two more a point over. {talent_certs} # Morale and burnout - Morale moves with pay against the going rate, your standing as an employer, burnout, a recent rise and where they work. It pulls the game's satisfaction a few points a day. - Burnout builds over a {talent_long} hour week and eases on lighter days. Burnt out people call in sick, and in the end hand in their notice. # Reviews and promotion - Everyone is reviewed {talent_reviews} times a year, rated 1 to 5. A 4 asks for a {talent_ask} rise and a 5 for {talent_ask_top}. Answer within {talent_ask_days} days or it counts as refused. - A rating of {talent_rating} or more, {talent_promote_days} days at the level and a skill near the next level opens a promotion with a {talent_promote_pay} rise. - A rise or a promotion you give comes at most once in {talent_rise_days} days for each person, and no wage the mod sets goes above {talent_wage_cap} times the game's usual pay for that person's skill. # Contracts - Probation lasts {talent_probation} days, with {talent_probation_notice} days of notice and no severance. - After it, notice is {talent_notice} days a year of service, at most {talent_notice_most}. A lay-off pays {talent_severance} week of pay a year of service, {talent_severance_least} weeks at least. - A dismissal without severance is fair only on probation or after {talent_low_runs} ratings of 1 in a row. - A restraint clause costs a {talent_clause} rise and cuts a rival's approaches by {talent_clause_poach}. # Rivals - Rivals go after seniors and above, more often when morale is low and pay is under the going rate. They offer {talent_poach_premium} more. Match it or they go, after their notice. You have {talent_poach_days} days to answer.

reallife_guide_tech_jobs_about: One labour market for the whole city: post ads for professionals, screen, interview and make offers, brief a search firm for senior people, and get more candidates from the recruitment office.
reallife_guide_tech_jobs: # The labour market - Between {hire_seekers_least} and {hire_seekers_most} professionals look for work at once: more in a slump, and {hire_graduates} more juniors in the summer. {hire_unemployment} - Each looks for a few weeks and then finds work elsewhere. The city's companies post about {hire_rivals} ads at a time and take seekers from the same list: whoever a rival takes is gone for you. - Engineers, data people, security and infrastructure staff are scarce, and seniors are few. The Market tab shows each family's seekers, openings, shortage and going rate. # The recruitment office - It stays the proper way to hire. For a professional skill it brings what you ask for and at least {hire_office_more} more besides, or {hire_office_share} more if that is more, picked from the city's seekers for the role your business needs, at {hire_office_floor} skill or more. - Its candidates wait in the game's own staff app, with the game's own pay talk. # The jobs board - The Jobs tab of Open Roles posts an ad for any professional role at any of your businesses: the level, the pay, the skill asked, where they work and for {hire_ad_days} days, at {hire_ad_day} a day. A boosted ad costs {hire_boost} times as much and is seen by twice as many. At most {hire_ads_most} ads run at once. - A week of an ad brings at most {hire_week} applicants, {hire_week_boosted} boosted. Who applies depends on the pay against their ask, where they would work, your standing as an employer and the rivals' ads in the same family. # Applicants - A CV may claim up to {hire_claim} points of skill too many. References cost {hire_refs} and say how the CV holds up; a background check costs {hire_background} and shows a past conviction. - An interview has {hire_rounds} questions. A technical one shows the true skill, one about pay shows their ask. A good interview makes them keener. - An offer of {hire_accept} of their ask or more is taken, less for a keen applicant and a good employer. From {hire_counter} they come back with their ask. In a scarce family another company may have offered {hire_rival_offer} more by then. A counter not answered in {hire_offer_days} days is a no; an application not acted on lapses after {hire_lapse} days. - Whoever is in work starts after their notice. A role the game has starts as the game's own employee at your business; a job done from home, or a role the game has not, starts on the payroll. # Search firms - For {hire_search_level} roles and above. A search costs {hire_search_fee} of a year's pay, {hire_search_retainer} when it starts and the rest on a hire, and brings {hire_search_count} candidates who are not on the open market in {hire_search_least} to {hire_search_most} days. - A data centre's crew has a search of its own, briefed from your headquarters: on the Search tab, or from a data centre's page on the Tech app's Infra tab. Pick the centre, technicians or network engineers, junior to staff level, and up to {crew_most} people (at first, what its racks lack). The fee is {crew_fee_least} to {crew_fee_most} of a year's pay a hire by level, a third now and the rest as each starts. The candidates come in {crew_days_least} to {crew_days_most} days, and those hired start at that data centre, on the payroll.
